name: Psoralen (PUVA, bergamot oil tanning)
summary: A plant-derived photosensitizer that supercharges tanning under UVA; used medically as PUVA, but its tanning use was banned for phototoxic and cancer concerns.
lead: Psoralen is the parent compound of the linear furanocoumarins, plant-derived photosensitizing chemicals that bind DNA when exposed to UVA light. They occur in figs, celery, parsley, citrus fruit and, in the form of bergapten and bergamottin, in bergamot oil .

name: Nasal tanning spray
summary: Needle-free melanotan sprays sold online; unlicensed, unregulated and untested by any published nasal-route study.
lead: Nasal tanning sprays are unlicensed products, sold online, that contain melanotan-type peptides intended to darken skin when sprayed into the nose rather than injected. The active ingredients are synthetic analogues of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), such as melanotan II .

name: Sunbed + MT2 stack
summary: Pairing unlicensed melanotan with tanning beds to rush pigment; two documented-risk exposures and no trial of the combination.
lead: The sunbed plus MT2 stack is a looksmaxxing practice of combining indoor tanning sessions with melanotan II (MT2), an unlicensed alpha-MSH analogue, with the stated goal of building pigment faster than either alone .

name: Primer tan / base tan
summary: Tanning in advance to avoid burns later; a UV-induced tan gives only modest protection (around SPF 3) and comes from the same DNA damage.
lead: A primer tan or base tan is a tan acquired before a holiday or sun-heavy period, in the belief that it will protect the skin from later sunburn. It is commonly gained through gradual sun exposure or tanning bed sessions .

name: Red light tan myth
summary: The idea that red-light devices can 'prime' skin to tan is discussed online, but no published study on it turned up.
lead: The red light tan claim is the belief, circulated in looksmaxxing and skincare circles, that treating skin with red or near-infrared light before UV exposure primes it to tan more readily. It is a fringe idea in the sense that its proponents rely mostly on informal reasoning rather than published research.

name: Tan lines meta
summary: Deliberately showing, hiding or evening out tan lines for a better-looking tan, a style detail with no clinical research behind it.
lead: Tan lines are visible boundaries between tanned skin and skin that was covered, for example by swimwear or a watch strap. In appearance-focused communities, the term 'tan lines meta' refers to deliberately managing them, either to avoid them for an even tan or to display them.

name: Vitamin D / UVB for tan
summary: The overlap between sun-for-vitamin-D and sun-for-a-tan: UVB does both, but they are separate goals.
lead: Vitamin D / UVB for tan refers to the overlap between exposing skin to ultraviolet B radiation for vitamin D production and doing so to obtain a tan. UVB converts a precursor in the skin into vitamin D3, which for most people supplies more vitamin D than diet.

name: Tanning oil
summary: Oils applied before sun exposure to deepen a tan, often with little or no SPF; sunless DHA oils also exist.
lead: Tanning oil is a cosmetic oil applied to the skin while sunbathing, traditionally intended to encourage tanning. Wikipedia credits Jean Patou's 1927 'Huile de Chaldee' as the first sun tan oil and notes baby oil was widely used in the 1950s to increase tanning.

name: Tanning drops (Isle of Paradise style)
summary: Self-tan concentrate drops mixed into a moisturiser to build a custom colour, with no independent research on them.
lead: Tanning drops are concentrated sunless tanning products designed to be mixed into moisturiser, serum or other skincare, letting the user adjust colour intensity. The format is associated with brands such as Isle of Paradise.

name: Tanning wipes / towelettes
summary: Pre-soaked DHA wipes for quick self-tan application; temporary colour with no published clinical trials.
lead: Tanning wipes, or towelettes, are tissues pre-soaked with a self-tanning or bronzing composition for application by wiping. A patent filing describes a tanning aid made of tissue paper impregnated with a tanning lotion, tanning oil or bronzing agent.

name: Body makeup / leg makeup
summary: Wash-off colour that evens tone and darkens skin for photos; a cosmetic with no trial evidence behind it.
lead: Body makeup, often sold as leg makeup, is a cosmetic applied to the skin of the body to even out tone, cover blemishes or add colour for a photo or event. It belongs to the family of temporary tints and bronzers, which wash off with soap and water.

name: Tan-extender moisturizer
summary: Hydrating lotion sold to stretch out a self-tan; the claim is untested.
lead: Tan-extender moisturizers are hydrating lotions marketed to prolong the colour of a sunless (self) tan. Self-tan colour from dihydroxyacetone (DHA) sits in the dead outer layer of skin and is described as fading over roughly 3 to 10 days as that layer is shed. Extender products are positioned as slowing that fade, and some contain small amounts of DHA to top up colour.

name: Exfoliating before tanning
summary: Scrubbing before self-tan to avoid patches; a common routine with no trials behind it.
lead: Exfoliating before tanning is the practice of scrubbing or otherwise removing dead surface skin before applying self-tanner, in the belief that it produces a more even colour. Sunless tanners based on dihydroxyacetone (DHA) are described as reacting with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin.
claims: Exfoliating first gives a more even self-tan.

name: Instagram tan filter / photo editing
summary: Editing or filters to look tanner in photos; part of the wider beauty-filter trend.
lead: Editing or lighting photos to look tanner is a form of digital appearance enhancement in which colour grading, filters or retouching apps darken or warm skin tone in images. It sits within the broader category of social media beauty filters, which smooth skin, reshape features and apply virtual makeup.

name: Sunless tan injections ('tan jabs')
summary: Unlicensed melanotan injections for tanning; flagged by health agencies since 2007 and linked to mole changes.
lead: "Tan jabs" are unlicensed injectable products, usually called melanotan, sold online and in some gyms and salons to darken skin without sun exposure. They are synthetic analogues of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), which drives melanin production.

name: Tanning gummies / supplements
summary: Carotenoid chews and pills sold to deepen a tan; no tanning approval and past retinal and liver concerns.
lead: Tanning gummies and supplements are oral products marketed to boost or deepen a tan, typically containing carotenoids such as beta-carotene. A related older category, tanning pills, used canthaxanthin, a carotenoid that deposits in body fat and gives a golden-orange tint.

name: Indoor tanning salon sessions
summary: Paying for timed UV bed or booth sessions to get a cosmetic tan, classed by the WHO's cancer agency as a carcinogen.
lead: Indoor tanning salon sessions are timed uses of ultraviolet (UV) tanning beds or vertical booths, usually in a commercial salon, to produce a cosmetic tan. The devices use fluorescent or high-pressure lamps that emit mostly UVA with a small amount of UVB.

name: Heliotherapy sunlamp
summary: Old-style home UV sunlamps, once sold for tanning and skin therapy, now studied mainly for their link to skin cancer.
lead: A sunlamp is an electric lamp that emits ultraviolet (UV) radiation, used for cosmetic tanning and, in clinical form, for phototherapy of skin conditions such as psoriasis, eczema and vitiligo. The term heliotherapy, literally sun treatment, historically referred to using sunlight or its artificial equivalent for therapy.

name: Intense pulsed light (IPL photofacial)
summary: A broad-spectrum flashlamp treatment used in clinics for sun spots, redness and thread veins, and also sold as home hair-removal devices.
lead: Intense pulsed light (IPL) is a skin-treatment technology in which a computer-controlled xenon flashlamp emits pulses of broad-spectrum light, roughly 400 to 1,200 nanometres, through filters that remove much ultraviolet and long infrared light. Unlike single-wavelength lasers, it can be tuned for different targets using interchangeable filters.

name: Q-switched / picosecond laser for pigment
summary: Ultra-short-pulse lasers used in clinics to break up pigment such as sun spots, melasma and tattoo ink; clinic-based, with limited published trial detail.
lead: Q-switched and picosecond lasers are pulsed lasers whose very short pulses are used in dermatology to fragment pigment. Q-switched devices emit pulses in the nanosecond range; picosecond devices are shorter still. Both are used for tattoo removal and, in clinics, for pigmented skin lesions such as lentigines and melasma.

name: Chemical peels (TCA, Jessner)
summary: Medium-depth acid peels, using trichloroacetic acid alone or after Jessner's solution, used by clinicians for photoaging, pigment and scars; DIY versions carry higher injury risk.
lead: Medium-depth chemical peels use trichloroacetic acid (TCA), sometimes in combination with Jessner's solution or glycolic acid, to produce a controlled injury to the epidermis and upper dermis. They are used in dermatology for photoaged skin, actinic keratoses, wrinkles, pigmentary disorders such as melasma and benign lesions, and atrophic acne scars.

name: Hydroquinone-tretinoin-steroid triple cream (Kligman formula)
summary: The classic prescription melasma cream combining hydroquinone, tretinoin and a corticosteroid; the best-studied topical for the condition, with trials mostly run on branded Tri-Luma.
lead: The hydroquinone-tretinoin-steroid triple combination cream, often called the Kligman formula, is a topical prescription treatment for melasma and other hyperpigmentation. It combines the skin-lightening agent hydroquinone, the retinoid tretinoin and a corticosteroid.

name: Thiamidol
summary: A lab-designed human-tyrosinase inhibitor in OTC dark-spot serums, with several 0.2% trials in melasma and PIH, mostly industry-linked.
lead: Thiamidol (isobutylamido thiazolyl resorcinol) is a synthetic resorcinol-derived compound developed as an inhibitor of human tyrosinase, the rate-limiting enzyme of melanin production. It is used in over-the-counter cosmetic serums and creams aimed at dark spots, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and melasma.

name: Licorice root extract (glabridin)
summary: A botanical lightener whose glabridin blocks tyrosinase in cell studies, but with no located human pigment trials.
lead: Licorice root extract, from Glycyrrhiza glabra, is a botanical ingredient used in cosmetic brightening products. Its main skin-active component is glabridin, a hydrophobic isoflavane found in the root extract.

name: Vitamin E / ferulic acid
summary: An antioxidant serum staple whose ferulic acid has lab-level antioxidant data but no located human brightening trials.
lead: Ferulic acid is a plant-derived hydroxycinnamic acid used in skincare as an antioxidant, commonly formulated alongside vitamin C and vitamin E in brightening and anti-aging serums. This entry covers the antioxidant combination in that context.

name: Lemon juice on skin
summary: A folk spot-lightener with no trials behind it and a documented citrus-plus-sunlight reaction that can leave lasting dark marks.
lead: Applying lemon juice to the skin is a folk home remedy used to lighten dark spots, freckles and marks, based on the belief that citrus acidity or vitamin C fades pigment.
claims: Lemon juice fades dark spots and freckles

name: Cica / Centella asiatica
summary: The gotu kola plant behind 'cica' skincare, a traditional soothing herb with no located trials for pigment recovery.
lead: Cica is the common skincare shorthand for Centella asiatica, a perennial herb in the Apiaceae family also called gotu kola or Asiatic pennywort. Extracts and isolated triterpenoids are used in soothing creams and serums, including products marketed for skin recovery after blemishes.

name: Oral cysteine / NAC for pigment
summary: A glutathione-precursor supplement claimed to lighten skin, with established medical uses but no located pigment studies.
lead: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is a prodrug of the amino acid L-cysteine, which is a precursor of the antioxidant glutathione. Some people in appearance and skin-lightening circles take oral NAC or cysteine in the belief that raising glutathione will lighten skin pigment.
claims: Taking NAC or cysteine raises glutathione and lightens skin

name: Sun avoidance / hat protocol
summary: Shade, brimmed hats and UPF clothing on top of sunscreen to keep melasma and photoageing at bay; sun is a documented trigger, hat protocols themselves are untested.
lead: Sun avoidance, often paired with wide-brimmed hats, is a skincare practice in which people minimise ultraviolet (UV) and sometimes visible-light exposure to the face, most commonly to prevent or control melasma and to slow visible skin ageing. It goes beyond routine sunscreen use to include staying in shade, avoiding midday sun, and wearing hats, sunglasses and protective clothing.
claims: Strict sun avoidance prevents melasma from returning
Total sun avoidance has no downside

name: Sunscreen + vitamin C layering routine
summary: Vitamin C serum under sunscreen in the morning; a common brightening routine with plausible rationale but no trials of the pairing itself.
lead: The sunscreen and vitamin C layering routine is a daytime skincare habit in which a topical vitamin C (ascorbic acid or a derivative) serum is applied first and a broad-spectrum sunscreen is applied over it. It is commonly described as a brightening and anti-ageing routine.
claims: Vitamin C under sunscreen adds extra protection against sun damage
